paragraphs.heading: A tsunami made by weather
paragraphs.text: A meteotsunami is a sea wave that behaves like a tsunami but is caused by the weather. It forms when air pressure changes quickly and shoves a body of water out of place. Severe thunderstorms, squalls and storm fronts can all produce such quick pressure swings. In some parts of the world these waves are common enough to have local names, such as rissaga in Catalan and abiki in Japanese.

paragraphs.heading: Hard to tell apart
paragraphs.text: Apart from their cause, meteotsunamis are so like ordinary tsunamis that telling them apart can be hard, for example when a tsunami wave appears with no earthquake, landslide or eruption on record. An ordinary tsunami usually comes from one sudden push, while a moving weather disturbance works on the ocean for a limited time, from several minutes to several hours. Only about 3% of recorded tsunamis from 2000 BC through 2014 are known to have come from weather. The real share may be much higher, since 10% of past tsunamis have unknown causes and some meteotsunamis may have been wrongly labelled as seiches, waves with slower changes in water level that stay within enclosed or partly enclosed basins.

paragraphs.heading: How they grow
paragraphs.text: Meteotsunamis usually happen when bad weather moves toward the coast at the same speed and in the same direction as the local waves. Shallow continental shelves, bays and inlets make the wave bigger. Places where the water's natural resonance frequency matches that of the waves are especially exposed, such as long, narrow bays whose mouth faces the incoming wave. Among the most susceptible areas are the Western Mediterranean, the eastern Adriatic Sea and Nagasaki Bay.

paragraphs.heading: Size and how often
paragraphs.text: They lack the energy of major earthquake tsunamis, so their effects stay local, but when resonance amplifies them they can be dangerous. An event can last from a few minutes to a couple of hours, and its size and length depend heavily on how fast and how severe the storm front is. Waves above 6 feet (1.8 m) have occurred, and the flooding can look like a storm surge. In April 2019 NOAA found that about 25 meteotsunamis strike the US East Coast each year on average, and the Great Lakes see about 126 a year.

paragraphs.heading: Deadly waves
paragraphs.text: In 1929 a 6-metre wave dragged ten people from the shore to their deaths at Grand Haven, Michigan. In 1954 a 3-metre wave swept people off piers on the Chicago waterfront, and seven drowned. On 31 March 1979 a meteotsunami in Nagasaki Bay peaked at 5 metres and killed three people.

paragraphs.heading: The 2013 East Coast event
paragraphs.text: In June 2013 a derecho just off New Jersey set off a meteotsunami that reached far along the coast. Tide gauges on the East Coast, in Puerto Rico and in Bermuda recorded conditions resembling a tsunami. At Newport, Rhode Island, the water peaked 1 foot above normal. At Barnegat Inlet in New Jersey, a six-foot wave pulled divers over a breakwater and swept three people off a jetty, seriously injuring two.
